strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: integrating spoken interaction and robot control so an agent can answer questions, execute actions, and respond to interruptions within one streaming architecture.

SA-MoE provides a coherent mechanism for combining pretrained speech and action experts through shared attention and modality-specific parameters. The implementation and staged training strategy are reasonably well explained.
Basic-task results are promising: ELLSA achieves 89.4% average LIBERO success and stronger speech-to-speech scores than the two evaluated speech baselines across all four benchmarks.

The evaluation extends beyond isolated tasks to concurrent speaking and acting, instruction rejection, interruptions, and context-grounded questions. Reporting individual-expert results and performance degradation during concurrent tasks is useful.
weaknesses: The central real-time full-duplex claim lacks operational validation. The model uses one-second blocks, but the paper reports no measured inference throughput, wall-clock response latency, interruption-to-stop latency, or execution hardware configuration. Responding within one second of a question ending does not establish timely interaction when computation and queued action execution are included.

The architectural comparison is substantially confounded. Appendix F compares two pretrained experts adapted with LoRA for 500 steps against single-expert initializations fully fine-tuned for 3,000 steps, with different training-task mixtures. Parameter capacity, initialization, optimization, and training exposure therefore differ. These experiments do not isolate the benefit of shared attention or substantiate lower training cost without compute measurements and controlled ablations.

There is no modular baseline combining speech recognition, the pretrained action policy, and a conversational model with interruption handling. Such a comparison is essential to establish the practical benefit of end-to-end integration and qualify claims that the demonstrated behaviors were previously unattainable. The incremental architectural contribution beyond attention-connected experts such as those in π0 also needs sharper positioning.

The advanced-task evaluation is narrow and provides limited evidence of generalization. Interruption training and testing use synthesized versions of the same ten commands; context-grounded VQA contains only twelve questions over nine LIBERO LONG tasks, without a clearly documented held-out question or scene protocol. There are no advanced-task baselines, and the rejection evaluation does not assess justification correctness. Natural speech, acoustic interference, and physical robot execution remain untested.

Claims of preserving expert performance and mitigating interference need qualification. Table 8 shows TriviaQA accuracy falling from 55.9 to 45.2 and LIBERO LONG success from 94.0% to 84.4% after integration. During concurrent interaction, LONG success falls further to 73.2%, while TriviaQA S2S falls from 41.7 to 30.7. These substantial losses warrant targeted ablations and failure analysis.

Evaluation reliability and reproducibility remain incomplete. Results lack uncertainty estimates or repeated-run analysis, and important details of task mixing and advanced-task data construction are missing. Similar aggregate manual and Gemini VQA accuracies do not establish judge reliability: Table 11 contains substantial per-question disagreements, and annotation-level agreement is not reported. Code and checkpoints are only promised upon acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: integrating spoken interaction and robot control while supporting questions and interruptions during execution. ELLSA is a useful systems contribution with a coherent architecture and training pipeline.

The reported results demonstrate substantial capability: 89.4% average LIBERO success with spoken instructions, strong speech-to-speech QA performance against the evaluated baselines, and approximately 83% context-grounded VQA accuracy.

The evaluation covers both individual capabilities and concurrent speaking and acting. Appendix F includes dense-model comparisons and individual-expert results, and the paper provides useful implementation details and evaluation prompts.
weaknesses: The central claim of real-time, full-duplex interaction lacks wall-clock evidence. The model processes one-second blocks, but no inference throughput, end-to-end response latency, or physical stopping latency is reported. Predicting 'Action Cancelled' and passing a turn-taking criterion do not establish prompt interruption of an executing action chunk.

The architectural comparisons do not isolate SA-MoE's contribution. In Appendix F, SA-MoE combines two pretrained experts and uses LoRA for 500 steps on all tasks, whereas dense baselines start from one expert and undergo full finetuning for 3,000 steps on basic tasks. Differences in pretrained capabilities, total capacity, optimization, and task mixture confound claims about modality interference and training efficiency; step counts alone do not establish lower computational cost.

The advanced tasks lack meaningful alternative-system baselines, such as a speech assistant connected to a VLA through transcription and an interruption controller. Consequently, the experiments establish feasibility but do not demonstrate the advantage of unified attention over simpler integration approaches. The novelty relative to the acknowledged attention-connected experts in π0 also needs sharper characterization.

Generalization evidence is narrow. Manipulation is evaluated only in LIBERO simulation; interruption training and testing use synthesized versions of the same ten commands; and context-grounded VQA comprises twelve questions over nine tasks without clearly documented held-out question or scene splits. No visual-input ablation establishes whether VQA answers require current observations rather than task-progress priors.

Claims of preserving specialist performance understate meaningful degradation. Table 8 shows TriviaQA dropping from 55.9 to 45.2 and LIBERO LONG from 94.0% to 84.4%; simultaneous speaking and acting further reduces LONG success to 73.2%. These tradeoffs deserve greater emphasis and analysis.

Evaluation reliability and reproducibility remain incomplete. Results lack confidence intervals or variation across training seeds; defective-instruction justifications are not formally scored; and similar aggregate human and Gemini VQA accuracy masks substantial per-question disagreement in Table 11. Advanced-task dataset sizes, sampling mixtures, and train/test separation are insufficiently specified. Together, these gaps leave the paper's broad claims insufficiently supported for acceptance.

strengths: ELLSA addresses a meaningful problem: integrating spoken interaction, visual perception, and robot actions in one streaming system. Concurrent dialogue and manipulation are valuable capabilities beyond conventional instruction-following policies.
The architecture is clearly motivated and technically plausible. Modality-specific pretrained experts communicate through shared attention, with LoRA providing a practical integration strategy.
Basic-task results are encouraging: ELLSA achieves 89.4% average LIBERO success with spoken instructions and exceeds both reported speech baselines on all four speech-to-speech evaluations.

The paper evaluates several useful interaction behaviors, including interruption handling, instruction rejection, and contextual questions during manipulation. Appendices provide substantial implementation details and acknowledge simulation-only validation.
weaknesses: The central real-time claim is not established. One-second temporal blocks describe sequence organization, but the paper reports no wall-clock inference throughput, speech latency, or command-to-physical-stop latency. Generating 'Action Cancelled' does not by itself establish prompt interruption of an executing action chunk.

The architectural comparison is substantially confounded. Appendix F compares two pretrained experts adapted with LoRA for 500 steps against single-expert initializations fully fine-tuned for 3,000 steps on a different task mixture. This does not isolate shared attention, specialization, or reduced modality interference, and training efficiency is not quantified in compute or GPU-hours.

There is no competitive baseline for the central concurrent-interaction tasks. A modular speech/VLM/controller system would help establish the benefit of end-to-end integration. Architectural novelty also needs sharper differentiation from the attention-connected experts in π0, which the paper explicitly builds upon.

Advanced-task evaluation is narrow and largely synthetic. Barge-in training and testing use synthesized instances of the same ten commands; contextual VQA covers only twelve questions across nine LIBERO LONG tasks, without a clearly documented held-out question/task protocol. These results provide limited evidence of generalization to natural interaction.

The strongest capability-preservation claims understate degradation. Compared with the individual experts, TriviaQA S2T falls from 55.9 to 45.2 and LIBERO LONG success from 94.0% to 84.4%. Concurrent interaction further reduces these to 35.1 and 73.2%, respectively. The stronger source action expert is absent from the main manipulation comparison.

Evaluation reliability and reproducibility remain incomplete: no repeated-training variability or confidence intervals are reported; instruction-rejection justifications are not assessed; and similar aggregate human/Gemini VQA scores conceal substantial per-question disagreements. Task-mixture proportions and advanced-task training-set sizes are also insufficiently specified. Overall, the promising integration does not yet have the controlled comparisons and deployment evidence needed for acceptance.

strengths: ELLSA addresses a meaningful problem: integrating streaming speech interaction with visual perception and robot control. Concurrent speech and action generation, contextual questions during execution, and spoken interruptions form a useful research direction.

The architecture is coherent and reasonably well described. Modality-specific pretrained transformers exchange information through shared attention, and the staged training procedure offers a practical way to combine existing capabilities.

Basic-task results are encouraging: ELLSA achieves 89.4% average success on LIBERO, strong speech-to-speech scores against the two evaluated speech baselines, and a 4.43 average task-chain length on CALVIN.

The appendix provides valuable implementation details and experiments, including comparisons with individual experts, block-duration and expert-count ablations, and a stronger speech encoder that substantially reduces concurrent-task degradation.
weaknesses: The central architectural and efficiency claims are not isolated by controlled comparisons. SA-MoE combines two pretrained experts, whereas each dense baseline starts from only one expert. The comparisons additionally change adaptation method, training duration, and task mixture: Appendix F describes 500 LoRA steps on all tasks versus 3,000 full-finetuning steps on basic tasks. Parameter budgets, training FLOPs, and wall-clock costs are not reported. These results demonstrate the usefulness of the complete integration recipe, but do not establish that shared-attention routing itself explains the gains or lowers total training cost.

Comparisons for the principal contribution are missing. The advanced interaction tasks evaluate only ELLSA, without a modular speech/VLM/VLA pipeline or another expert-fusion architecture. Because SA-MoE explicitly extends the attention-connected experts of π0, stronger comparisons are needed to establish the significance of the architectural extension and the claimed advantages over simpler system integration.

The full-duplex evaluation is substantially narrower than the claims. Turn-taking is judged by responding within one second after an utterance ends, while action interruption uses ten fixed command formulations synthesized separately for training and testing. Table 9 reports average per-block computation time, but not wall-clock interruption-to-stop latency, latency distributions, or joint speech-and-action execution timing. Natural overlapping speech, ambiguous pauses, unseen interruption wording, and acoustic interference are not evaluated. Thus, claims of immediate stopping and broadly natural full-duplex behavior remain insufficiently supported.

Evidence for grounded interaction generalization is limited. Contextual VQA uses only 12 questions associated with nine LIBERO LONG tasks, and the separation of training and evaluation questions, scenes, and annotations is insufficiently specified. Defective-command evaluation contains 160 examples and does not assess justification correctness. Without unseen task/question combinations and language-only or observation-removal controls, these evaluations do not establish robust visual grounding rather than exploitation of task and language regularities.

Claims of preserving specialist performance need qualification. Relative to the original experts, TriviaQA S2T accuracy drops from 55.9 to 45.2 and LIBERO LONG success from 94.0% to 84.4%. Concurrent speaking further reduces these scores to 35.1 and 73.2%, respectively. The stronger encoder improves this tradeoff, but does not establish that remaining interference is primarily a capacity issue rather than an architectural limitation.

Validation and reproducibility remain incomplete. All robot experiments are simulated, and CALVIN extends basic-task evaluation rather than the advanced interaction tests. Results lack repeated-run variability or confidence intervals. Training mixture proportions and construction details for several advanced tasks are missing. Similar aggregate human and Gemini VQA accuracy also does not establish evaluator reliability, especially given substantial per-question discrepancies in Table 15.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: integrating streaming speech interaction with visually grounded robot control. The unified system supports useful behaviors, including answering questions during manipulation and responding to interruption commands.

The reported results provide credible evidence of useful integration: 89.4% average LIBERO success, competitive speech QA performance, and a CALVIN variant achieving 4.43 consecutively completed tasks.

The appendices contain substantial supporting experiments, including comparisons with individual experts, dense baselines, different time-block durations, expert counts, and speech encoders. The stronger encoder substantially reduces the performance loss during concurrent speaking and acting.

Architecture, training stages, evaluation prompts, and several dataset construction details are documented. Measured inference times support the feasibility of processing each block within its duration.
weaknesses: The central architectural comparison is confounded. In Appendix F, SA-MoE combines two pretrained backbones and uses LoRA for 500 steps on all tasks, whereas dense baselines start from one expert and undergo full finetuning for 3,000 steps on basic tasks only. Differences in pretrained capabilities, total capacity, optimization, and task mixtures prevent attributing the gains specifically to SA-MoE or establishing its claimed training efficiency. Matched controls and actual compute accounting are needed.

The practical advantage over modular systems is untested. A streaming speech model combined with ASR-conditioned UniVLA, speech synthesis, and interruption handling would be an important baseline for the advanced tasks. Without this comparison, the results demonstrate an integrated implementation but do not establish that its interaction capabilities require the proposed architecture or were previously unattainable.

The full-duplex evaluation is substantially narrower than the claims. Turn-taking success is defined primarily by responding within one second after a question ends; this does not adequately test premature responses, hesitation, overlapping speech, or natural conversational timing. Barge-in training and testing use synthesized versions of the same ten command phrases. The 94.3% success rate therefore provides limited evidence of general interruption understanding.

Per-block inference latency does not establish end-to-end interruption responsiveness. Table 9 reports 786 ms for speech-to-action processing with one-second blocks, but the paper does not report command-to-physical-stop latency, its distribution, or how already-issued action chunks are cancelled. Producing 'Action Cancelled' is an insufficiently specified proxy for immediately stopping execution.

Evidence for grounded generalization is limited. Context-grounded VQA contains only 12 question templates across nine LIBERO LONG tasks, without clearly documented held-out question or scene generalization or controls that remove visual input. Defective-command evaluation contains 160 examples and does not assess justification correctness. The close aggregate manual and Gemini accuracies also conceal substantial per-question discrepancies in Table 15, weakening the claim that aggregate agreement validates the automatic evaluator.

Claims of preserving expert performance and mitigating interference need qualification. Table 8 shows TriviaQA accuracy falling from 55.9 to 45.2 and LIBERO LONG success from 94.0% to 84.4% after integration; concurrent speaking further reduces the latter to 73.2% in the main configuration. Although the stronger-encoder ablation helps, the paper lacks repeated-run uncertainty estimates and a controlled analysis explaining these losses. Overall, the promising system results do not yet resolve the main concerns about architectural attribution and interaction evaluation sufficiently for acceptance.

strengths: ELLSA addresses a meaningful problem: integrating streaming speech interaction with visual perception and robot control. The unified system supports useful behaviors, including speaking while acting, progress-related question answering, and spoken interruption.

The modality-specific experts connected through shared attention provide a coherent way to reuse pretrained speech and action models. The architecture and staged training procedure are described reasonably clearly.

The basic-capability results are substantial: ELLSA achieves 89.4% average success on LIBERO and outperforms the two evaluated speech baselines on all reported speech-to-speech metrics. The additional CALVIN results broaden the evidence beyond one manipulation benchmark.

The appendices include useful comparisons against individual experts and dense models, ablations of block duration and expert count, and an improved speech encoder that substantially reduces interference during simultaneous speaking and acting.
weaknesses: The architectural advantage is not cleanly isolated. In Table 7, SA-MoE combines two pretrained experts, whereas each dense baseline starts from only one; training methods, task mixtures, and parameter budgets also differ. These results demonstrate the value of the complete integration recipe but do not establish that shared-attention routing itself explains the gains or training efficiency. A modular speech/VLA pipeline and more closely matched architectural baselines are missing.

The strongest novelty claims exceed the evidence. Attention-connected experts explicitly build on π0, and interleaving modalities is an incremental mechanism. The potentially important contribution is their integration into an interactive system, but claims that these behaviors were previously unattainable require stronger positioning and comparisons, particularly against modular systems.

The full-duplex evaluation is narrow. Turn-taking is primarily assessed by whether a response occurs within one second after a question ends, and interruption training and testing use synthesized versions of the same ten commands. The reported per-block inference times do not establish end-to-end interruption latency, physical stopping time, or reliable operation with natural overlapping speech. No real-robot validation is provided.

The advanced grounding evidence is limited: context-grounded VQA contains only 12 questions across nine tasks, with no clearly documented held-out question or scene generalization protocol. Defective-instruction evaluation covers 160 examples and does not assess justification correctness. Similar aggregate human and Gemini accuracy does not establish evaluator agreement, especially given their substantial per-question discrepancies in Table 15.

Claims of matching specialized models and mitigating interference need qualification. The original action expert averages 95.45% LIBERO success versus ELLSA's 89.35%, while concurrent speaking reduces the default model's LONG success from 84.4% to 73.2%. The stronger encoder helps, but does not isolate model capacity as the cause. Missing uncertainty estimates and incomplete reporting of advanced-task training mixtures further limit interpretation. Overall, this is a promising systems contribution, but the comparison and interaction-evaluation gaps leave it slightly below the acceptance threshold.
